Revenue estimates were cut sharply as the analysts signalled a weaker outlook - perhaps a sign that investors should temper their expectations as well. At UK£2.82, shares are up 4.1% in the past 7 days. The consensus view seems to have become more pessimistic on Griffin Mining, noting the measurable cut to revenue estimates in this update.

data.title: Here's Why We're Watching Corcel's (LON:CRCL) Cash Burn Situation
data.description:
Even when a business is losing money, it's possible for shareholders to make money if they buy a good business at the right price. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. But while history lauds those rare successes, those that fail are often forgotten; who remembers Pets.com?

Given this risk, we thought we'd take a look at whether Corcel (LON:CRCL) shareholders should be worried about its cash burn. In this article, we define cash burn as its annual (negative) free cash flow, which is the amount of money a company spends each year to fund its growth. Let's start with an examination of the business' cash, relative to its cash burn.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Advertisement

How Long Is Corcel's Cash Runway?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. As at December 2025, Corcel had cash of UK£5.2m and such minimal debt that we can ignore it for the purposes of this analysis. In the last year, its cash burn was UK£5.9m. That means it had a cash runway of around 11 months as of December 2025. Importantly, the one analyst we see covering the stock thinks that Corcel will reach cashflow breakeven in 3 years. Essentially, that means the company will either reduce its cash burn, or else require more cash. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

View our latest analysis for Corcel

How Is Corcel's Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Corcel didn't record any revenue over the last year, indicating that it's an early stage company still developing its business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. In fact, it ramped its spending strongly over the last year, increasing cash burn by 123%. It's fair to say that sort of rate of increase cannot be maintained for very long, without putting pressure on the balance sheet. While the past is always worth studying, it is the future that matters most of all. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Easily Can Corcel Raise Cash?

Since its cash burn is moving in the wrong direction, Corcel shareholders may wish to think ahead to when the company may need to raise more cash. Companies can raise capital through either debt or equity. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. By comparing a company's annual cash burn to its total market capitalisation, we can estimate roughly how many shares it would have to issue in order to run the company for another year (at the same burn rate).

Corcel has a market capitalisation of UK£37m and burnt through UK£5.9m last year, which is 16% of the company's market value. As a result, we'd venture that the company could raise more cash for growth without much trouble, albeit at the cost of some dilution.

Is Corcel's Cash Burn A Worry?

On this analysis of Corcel's cash burn, we think its cash burn relative to its market cap was reassuring, while its increasing cash burn has us a bit worried. Shareholders can take heart from the fact that at least one analyst is forecasting it will reach breakeven. We don't think its cash burn is particularly problematic, but after considering the range of factors in this article, we do think shareholders should be monitoring how it changes over time. NuScale Power (SMR)

Overview: NuScale Power is a nuclear engineering company focused on its NuScale Power Module small modular reactor, a 77 MWe light water reactor design that comes bundled with full plant design, licensing support, construction, operations, and maintenance services for utilities seeking reliable baseload power. It also provides a wide range of regulatory, training, fuel management, and outage support services that extend across the full life cycle of a nuclear power plant.

Operations: NuScale Power currently generates its approximately US$11 million in revenue from electric utility related services in the United States.

Market Cap: US$3.9 billion

NuScale Power gives you direct exposure to the push for modular nuclear reactors, with its NRC certified NuScale Power Module and a pipeline that includes the TVA ENTRA1 program in the US and the RoPower project in Romania. The company reports strong liquidity of about US$1.9b and a mature supplier network, which supports its goal of moving from engineering work into full plant deployment, although it is still loss making and relies heavily on external funding and equity issuance. Execution risk around securing firm power purchase agreements and managing complex supply chains is real, yet if those hurdles are cleared, the combination of regulatory lead and global interest in dependable nuclear power could be powerful.

Oklo (OKLO)

Overview: Oklo develops Aurora fission power plants, a family of small modular reactors designed to deliver 15 to 75 MW of electricity for grid and industrial customers. It is tightly linked to the nuclear energy theme through its focus on owning and operating reactors rather than just selling equipment. The company is also working on nuclear fuel recycling and fabrication that can turn used nuclear fuel into fresh fuel for its own reactors.

Market Cap: US$7.7 billion

Oklo provides exposure to compact nuclear power at a time when data centers and industrial users are looking for dedicated, long term electricity supply, backed by a model that aims to sell power through contracts instead of one off reactor sales. Recent milestones such as regulatory progress on Aurora, first criticality at the Groves test reactor and early revenue around US$1.2 million indicate movement toward commercialisation. A cash position near US$3 billion provides funding capacity for that build out. On the other hand, Oklo is loss making, carries funding and dilution risk, has no commercial reactors running yet and still faces licensing hurdles, so the gap between large contracts and real, recurring cash flow is a key issue investors need to weigh carefully.

Oklo’s push to own and operate reactors, backed by around US$3b in cash, raises a big question about how that plan could translate into long term contracts and cash flow. Walk through the analyst forecasts for Oklo to see what the numbers hint at, but do not fully explain yet.

GE Vernova (GEV)

Overview: GE Vernova is an energy equipment and services company that supplies the hardware and software needed to generate, move, and manage electricity, with its Power segment designing and servicing gas, nuclear, hydro, and steam technologies used by utilities and industrial customers. For nuclear focused investors, the most direct link is its nuclear steam turbines, generators, and long term plant services that support the construction, operation, and maintenance of reactors within a broader portfolio that also includes wind and grid solutions.

Operations: GE Vernova generates revenue primarily from its Power segment at about US$21.0b, alongside roughly US$12.2b from Electrification and US$8.5b from Wind, with small intersegment eliminations.

Market Cap: US$257.3b

GE Vernova gives you exposure to the nuclear energy ecosystem through its turbine and generator equipment and decades long service contracts, while also tapping into AI driven electricity demand and grid upgrades. The company carries a large installed base, a sizeable backlog, and improving profitability, with analysts pointing to earnings and revenue growth expectations. However, you also need to weigh a wind segment that affects margins, reliance on external borrowing, and one off gains that can cloud the true earnings run rate. The mix of nuclear linked infrastructure, recurring service revenue, and a P/E below the broader electrical industry has attracted analyst attention. A key consideration is how durable that cash generation can be once one offs fade and wind challenges are addressed.
